pages.title: Modules in Python
pages.content: A Python module is a `.py` file that groups reusable code such as functions, classes, and variables. Another file can import the module and access its members through the module name.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Modules: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

codeCard.code:
# helpers.py
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}"

# main.py
import helpers
print(helpers.greet("Asha"))

checkpoint.question: What is a Python module?
options: A reusable Python file containing code
checkpoint.explanation: A module is a reusable Python file that can expose functions, classes, and variables.

pages.title: How to use modules in Python
pages.content: A module can be imported with `import module_name`. Python executes the module once when it is first imported, and the imported name refers to the module object.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Modules: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

pages.title: How to import specific parts from module
pages.content: The `from module import name` form brings selected names into the current namespace. An alias can also be used to make a name shorter or clearer.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Modules: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

codeCard.code:
from math import sqrt as root

print(root(49))

pages.title: Modules - MCQ
pages.content: Use module imports to reuse code instead of duplicating it. Prefer explicit imports that make dependencies easy to identify.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Modules: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

topics.title: Namespaces and Scope
topics.description: Learn Namespaces and Scope through focused explanations and practical Python examples.

pages.title: Scope in Python
pages.content: Python resolves names through nested scopes. A local name belongs to a function, an enclosing name belongs to an outer function, and a global name belongs to the module. The built-in namespace supplies names such as `len` and `print`.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Namespaces and Scope: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

codeCard.code:
x = 10

def show():
    x = 20
    print("Local:", x)

show()
print("Global:", x)

checkpoint.question: Which keyword allows a function to modify a module-level binding?
checkpoint.explanation: `global` tells Python that an assignment should rebind the name in the module-level namespace.

pages.title: Global Variable Modification
pages.content: Use the `global` keyword only when a function must rebind a module-level variable. Without `global`, assigning to a name inside a function creates or updates a local binding.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Namespaces and Scope: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

codeCard.code:
count = 0

def increment():
    global count
    count += 1

increment()
print(count)

pages.title: Namespace in Python
pages.content: A namespace maps names to objects. Functions create local namespaces, modules provide a global namespace, and Python also provides a built-in namespace.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Namespaces and Scope: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

codeCard.code:
value = 42
print("Global names include value:", "value" in globals())

def demo():
    local_value = 7
    print("Local names include local_value:", "local_value" in locals())

demo()

topics.title: Generators
topics.description: Learn Generators through focused explanations and practical Python examples.

pages.title: How to use for loop in generator functions
pages.content: A generator function uses `yield` to produce values lazily. A `for` loop consumes those values one at a time and automatically stops when the generator is exhausted.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Generators: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

checkpoint.question: What does a generator function return when it is called?
options: A list immediately containing every value
checkpoint.explanation: Calling a generator function creates a generator object; the body runs as iteration advances.

pages.title: Python Generators MCQ
pages.content: Calling a generator function does not execute its body immediately. It returns a generator object; execution advances when the generator is iterated.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Generators: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

codeCard.code:
def demo():
    print("started")
    yield 1

gen = demo()
print(type(gen).__name__)
print(next(gen))

pages.title: Generator Function Call Behavior
pages.content: Each `next()` resumes a generator where it last yielded. After the final yield, another `next()` raises `StopIteration`.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Generators: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

topics.title: Iterators
topics.description: Learn Iterators through focused explanations and practical Python examples.

pages.title: How to use iterators with for loop
pages.content: A `for` loop asks an iterator for one value at a time by repeatedly calling `__next__()` until `StopIteration` occurs.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Iterators: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

checkpoint.question: Which method provides the next value from an iterator?
checkpoint.explanation: `__next__()` returns the next item or raises `StopIteration` when exhausted.

pages.title: Iterator Methods Identification
pages.content: An iterator implements `__iter__()` and `__next__()`. Usually `__iter__()` returns the iterator itself, while `__next__()` returns the next value or raises `StopIteration`.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Iterators: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

pages.title: Iterator Method - MCQ
pages.content: An iterator becomes exhausted after its final value. Calling `next()` again raises `StopIteration`, which is how a `for` loop knows to stop.

topics.title: Regular Expressions
topics.description: Learn Regular Expressions through focused explanations and practical Python examples.

pages.title: RegEx in Python
pages.content: Python's `re` module provides regular-expression operations such as `search`, `findall`, `split`, and `sub`. Compile a pattern when you will reuse it multiple times.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Regular Expressions: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

codeCard.code:
import re

text = "Order 123, item 45"
print(re.findall(r"\d+", text))

checkpoint.question: Which `re` function returns all non-overlapping matches?
checkpoint.explanation: `re.findall()` returns a list of all non-overlapping matches.

pages.title: Sets in RegEx
pages.content: Character sets such as `[A-Z]`, `[0-9]`, and `[^0-9]` match one character from or outside a defined set.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Regular Expressions: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

codeCard.code:
import re

text = "A1 B2 C3"
print(re.findall(r"[A-Z]", text))

pages.title: Metacharacters in RegEx
pages.content: Metacharacters give regular expressions structure. For example, `.` matches a character, `^` anchors the start, `$` anchors the end, `*` repeats zero or more times, and `+` repeats one or more times.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Regular Expressions: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

text = "cat cart coat"
print(re.findall(r"c.t", text))

topics.title: Decorators

pages.title: Decorators - MCQ
pages.content: A decorator is a callable that receives a function or class and returns a replacement or wrapped version. It is commonly used to add behavior without editing the original function body.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Decorators: focus on the behavior demonstrated by this page and reproduce it with a small Python example.

checkpoint.question: What does the `@decorator` syntax do?
options: It replaces/rebinds a function with the decorator result
It converts Python to bytecode at runtime
checkpoint.explanation: The decorated function name is rebound to the value returned by the decorator.

pages.title: Decorator Function Behavior
pages.content: When Python evaluates `@decorator` above a function, it is equivalent to rebinding the function name to the result of `decorator(function)`.
